John Budd, M.D.

John Henry Budd, M.D. was born in Canada on December 6, 1908. A lifelong jazz enthusiast, music has always been his avocation. During his high school years he was employed playing the piano for a year in movie theaters, prior to the “talkies.” He has enjoyed a distinguished medical career, and is a former president of the AMA. Dr. Budd has enjoyed many friendships with jazz musicians throughout the years, and continues to attend jazz parties across the country.
Dr. Budd was interviewed at the Jerome Jazz Party in Aspen, Colorado on October 11, 1997, by Monk Rowe, director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.
Today we’re filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive in Aspen, Colorado, and I’m very happy to have Dr. John Budd, man of medicine and a jazz fan with a capital F — I think that’s safe to say.
Yeah, it is indeed.
In the little bit I’ve talked to you, I have actually learned that I don’t know nearly as much as I thought I did.
My. Isn’t that part of learning?
Yes I think so. Because your appreciation of the music seems to go way back. You are going to celebrate your 89th birthday in February is that correct?
In December.
In December. Well congratulations.
Thank you. It’s well to do it in advance at my age. Don’t jump too far ahead. Prophecy is dangerous.
Right. Well you have said to me a couple of times that your three main interests in your life have been medicine, music and baseball.
Exactly.
And that they are not so far apart as we might tend to think.
True.
Is that a place where we could start talking?

It’d be fine. Yes, because I feel that very strongly. The older I get the more I realize that the baseball has sort of left me behind because there have become millionaires and tremendous ability, but it’s become a business, no longer just a baseball game. And of course the same thing has happened in music. What’s happening in music is shocking to me at my age, and my tastes in music, and the same thing has happened in medicine. Medicine, which used to be a profession, now is like a business and it’s seen by the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -1-
competition in doctors, insurance companies, hospitals, patients, and lawyers, to get the best they can and provide the best they can, and it’s different.
Well the idea of a profession, are you saying that people don’t do it because they’re as passionate about it as they used to be?

Well that may be I don’t know. But there’s something to that, that the passion is — the passionate move is money, prestige and so forth. And the three professions I guess they used to tell us were medicine, law and the liturgy. Now professions are anything in the world. Professionalism means great ability. But it’s not only that, but professionalism is having a selfless attitude toward helping somebody else I think. Maybe that’s a mistake I have, and I’m not putting it down at all. But I’m glad to be considered one although when I talk to these musicians, if they are professional I am a ham.

No I think you’re right because one thing that people talk about, when you hear musicians talk about other musicians, and what a professional he is, they almost always mention that when they are playing the music, they are most concerned about how the whole thing sounds.
That’s exactly right, yes.
So that is their version of professionalism.

Well it’s a good one. It is indeed. And they are. And they do care for each other and they listen to each other and they don’t ever say out and out “he doesn’t play as well as I do.” They sometimes say “I wish I could do something as well as he did,” they envy each other, but they don’t put each other down very often. I don’t think they do.
Well how is music and medicine intertwined for you in your life?

Oh different ways. People — one small example of medicine and music would be Herman Chittison, the piano player, happens to be about my age. I had heard him many years ago when he was a Blue Note pianist on a program called the — some kind of photography — Flash Casey, Crime Photographer. It was from the radio, on Thursday nights. And the setting was in a place called the Blue Note. And every week it was a whodunnit thing. It was kind of interesting. But in the background music was this guy playing the piano. And I didn’t know who it was, but he became more popular than the program of people wondering who he is. It turned out it was Herman Chittison and he became known as the “Blue Note Pianist.” And I heard about that and I enjoyed his playing. I had a chance to meet him one time, many years later, about 1960 at a medical meeting and he was playing in the restaurant. And I went with another doctor friend because I wanted to hear him play and see him. I listened to him and talked to him and we became friends, and later he came to Cleveland and worked in a Stoeffer’s Restaurant there, and I went down to see him and all that. And he happened to come to me as a patient one time. He says “you are a doctor and I enjoyed talking to you and I have some © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

indigestion and I’d like to see you about it.” I had a GI X-ray series and incidentally a chest X-ray, which was sort of routine in those days to make sure your chest, you didn’t have tuberculosis at least. And the radiologist said “this little thing in this lung there that looks bad to me if it was never there before it’s new and it’s dangerous. If it’s been there before it may be a calcified lymph node and don’t worry about it, see if you can get an old film.” So we got one from Akron, six months before, and it wasn’t seen then, so it’s new. And he said it doesn’t sound good. It’s in the middle of the lung and you can’t do a bronchoscopic examination, you have to do an exploratory in there. And Herman didn’t like that and he put it off. And we talked a lot. He’d come to my house and he would play the piano and we’d talk about music and he’d show me chords and so forth. And we’d get back to saying Herman it’s time to go and see the doctor. He finally, after about three months, he said “I think I’d better go and get that done, where shall I go?” And I said “go up to the University Hospital in Cleveland, they’re experts there and the Cleveland Clinic is very famous, you’ll find great people there.” He said “where do you go?” And I told him Deaconess Hospital. And he said “is there anybody there that does this kind of work well?” And I said “yes I know a young man who was in the Army and trained after the war with the clinic people, and he’s the head of our staff and he’s pretty good and he’s young and he’s a good friend.” So he said “well I’ll go to him.” And he went and had a lobectomy — part of one of his lungs removed — and the doctor said “this is only palliative, it’s not curative because it’s beyond where I can...” But Herman went back to work and played about a year. He finally got sick and got very short of breath. He came to see me, went to the hospital and in another day or so was dead. But that’s medicine and that sort of thing. And medicine-baseball: one time in my job as a doctor, the AMA and the House of Delegates, they wanted an insurance program for some of the doctors. There was a program at that time for disability for doctors or employees of doctors, and if you’re disabled well you get your benefits. But it was a generous one because you have to be so disabled that you can’t do your ordinary job, what you ordinarily do. And it turns out some doctors say “I’m seventy years old, I’m no longer able to do surgery I don’t think, but I can still practice medicine but I can’t do surgery, so I should have my disability.” And they argued about that, and the insurance policy exactly said you’ve got to be paid. So they almost went broke until that program ran out and then they looked for somebody else to give them coverage, and they got that Charlie Findlay who ran an insurance company, and he began going around to telephone the doctors in Michigan, in New Jersey, in Texas, in California, Ohio — the larger states where they had a lot of doctors to find somebody in that state that was fairly well known that might exert some influence to persuade the AMA perhaps to buy his particular policy. And I got to know him and he happened to say in this conversation “do you like baseball?” I said my © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-

goodness he said the magic word. So he said when you come to New York I’d like to see you and we’ll go to a game together. We became great friends. And one evening, in Chicago, I saw him at an AMA meeting and we went out to dinner together with another doctor. We went to one of these places where they had dine and dance and a band played there, and I got to play with this orchestra for fun, and he was quite impressed about that. And he became a great friend and I’ve known him until the day he died. So that was medicine and baseball.
He owned one of the baseball teams, right?

At the time I knew him, he had bought the Kansas City team which then moved to Oakland. And he had an office in Chicago, and I’ve been there several times, and he closed his office business at four in the afternoon but at that time out in California it was only maybe two or three. He could listen and he’d talk, I remember him talking to Joe Kronin on the telephone and giving advice about things. And he had one day a young player from Ohio, Gene Tenace was his name, was a great catcher, a new player, and Charlie Findlay had another friend and I down to a fish fry in his office one night, and he had this young baseball player there, we met him, and Tenace — Findlay won three or four pennants in a row and a couple of World Series. And Tenace happened to hit two home runs in the first game or something, a lot of home runs, became quite famous. I’ve never seen him since, but I happened to meet that guy in baseball, partly through Findlay and partly through medicine. And also about health I know that Charlie Findlay had a coronary and had some medical treatment, not by me, but I saw him when he was sick in Chicago where he lived. But the three just seem to intermingle many, many, many times.
So you were born in 1911?
December.
My math isn’t quite up to snuff. And when you were a young man, what kind of music was the music of the day?

I had classical music piano lessons. I went to a neighbor who was a piano teacher and subsequent teachers and just learned to play music, and then finally went to the Conservatory in Halifax. They had young ladies mostly who were studying and you would employ one of them to teach you at good rates I guess, and you’d have one for a year and then she would go on to the next grade and I’d get another one. But I got the same thing again. So I learned how to read, how to put fingering into exercises, and how to memorize, but nothing about anything about tone or quality or things like that. And I got to be very good at it because you do it in a practice stall. After, when I became 13, my mother said maybe high school may be a little too much for you. I took advantage of © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

that and said I think it is, I’ve had enough. So we quit. I took two years, I went to high school and in a couple of years there was a show put on and they had some people to play music, and there was not a piano player maybe. They got me to play and I began to play, and learned tunes like that. The birds are singing/I’ll feather your nest and songs like that. And all these old, old songs that day. And then when I went into college I was looking for a job and my father one day was walking down the street, I had a job one year working at City Hall working as a filing clerk in my first year in college, and at the first intermission after that Dad said to me walking down the street, “I think you could probably play the piano in a moving picture theater.” And I was shocked. I thought he doesn’t know anything about music and he’s dreaming. So he asked the manager if he would be interested and he said “come down and see me.” He come in and he listened to me and said “come down this afternoon” — this is Thursday— “and finish out this week and if you do all right we’ll hire you.” And at that time I had read Horatio Alger stories — you ever heard of him?
Sure.

And when the boy struck it rich, some rich guy up in New York came around and gave him ten dollars a week and that was big money. And so I said to Mr. Acker, I didn’t like to be presumptuous, but Mr. Acker, how much do you pay? I thought if he said ten dollars a week I might ask for fifteen. He said “we pay thirty dollars a week.” That was big money in 1926. And he said “we have union scale, it’s a dollar an hour, but we don’t have a union but we pay it. And you play five hours a day.” I played the off hours when not many people would be there listening, from one to three, the regular guy from three to five, I played five to seven, and the other man seven to nine, I played nine to ten, and he played ten to eleven. So it was five hours a day, six days week, at a dollar an hour is thirty dollars week. And that was the end of that.
That’s hard work too.
Well if you play some five hours a day for three months you have to get better. So I became fairly agile at playing the piano.
Was this where you sat and watched the film?
Yes.
And so what were you using for music? Was it partly improvised?

The theater had a library of music, and with every film a cue sheet would come with it with the name of the film, the producer, the director and the cast and all these things, and suggested music for the introduction music. And then they have incidents that happen. Like boy and girl meet and love each other or something like that and you’d play — one of the favorites in those days was “Whispering Hope” that was the first time I ever heard the tune, that was on one of the cue sheets. And there were also mysterisos and agitatos © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

and gallops and furiosos and different styles, just specific music written for that purpose. You see they say mysterious cowboy appears in window. One minute and a half. Agitato or mysterioso number three. And you’d look in the library, if they had it you’d try to play it. If they didn’t, make up something like that or something that you knew. And for news reels you’d play marches. For comedies you’d play comic songs like “Barney Google” or something like that. And then it was probably pretty desperate I think but it stayed and lasted 13 weeks.
Right. And then they learned to put the sound on the film.

Yes, the next year. In 1926. In 1927 I started again at the same place, the Orpheus Theater in Halifax, and part time, a relief pianist, when other guys would go on vacation — or would play at the Imperial Theater across the street, and also the King Edward Theater up in the north end of the town, and you’d play maybe a week with each of them until about August and then the talkies came in and that was the end of the job.
When did you first become aware of jazz music?

I suppose in college. My roommate happened to be from Nova Scotia. And he was a saxophone player, but a C melody saxophone. He got me interested in it. He knew players by name, and he worshipped Eddie Miller, even in those days, in the 19 — what was those years — 1931 or 32, and different people. And he talked about them. Of course he played the C melody saxophone, which I don’t know is even made now, but Frankie Trumbauer did play that, and Freddie McClelland was his name. The interesting thing about him, he lived across the street from Dr. Dan Murray, whose son Carson Murray is the father of Anne Murray who sings, the Canadian girl, and her, Doc Murray’s — Carson Murray’s younger brother, Don Murray, was a classmate of mine in Arts & Science school, and a marvelous piano player, and cornet player. And a marvelous musician. He wrote many songs and words, college songs and so forth. And he was a character, a marvelous person. And one of the things, there was a movie in those days, when those talkies came out, where there was a little band and there was about a five piece band, and the fellow who was playing the piano, or seemed to be in the movie, played the left hand on the piano and played the trumpet in the right hand. And Don Murray learned to do that. Although it’s a different key of course, the trumpet is in B flat, the piano is in another key, and Don did that, and he’d write songs and plays and poetry and I got to know him very well. Carson, his brother, was one year ahead of me in medical school, who was Anne’s father. I had never heard of Anne Murray until later, my son, who was in the same college with her at that time, said he’d met this girl, Anne Murray. And I had never heard of her. He said “well she’s famous, you should know her.” And her brother was a roommate of my young son in college there, in medical school. And he’s now practicing in Antignish I think, one of them. She had two or three © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-

brothers, and I think they’ve sung with her since. I met her one time just by asking where she was in Las Vegas and her manager said to come and see the show and come downstairs in the dressing room later. And I went down and she was very gracious and listened and answered questions and finally said “well why did you particularly want to see me?” I said “well I’ve heard about you and my son talked about you.” And she said “what’s his name?” I said “Charles.” “Oh Charlie Budd, yes I know all about him.” But she didn’t know me. But she has still become a star and just within the past week she had a program on: An Evening With Anne Murray. I didn’t see it but I bet it was good.
Yeah. She’s a wonderful singer.
She’s got character and class, great.
You were in college in what city?
Halifax. Nova Scotia.
When was the first time that you got to see a well known jazz band? Was it there or was it somewhere else?

New York. After I finished that job in the theater, my mother suggested that I should have a vacation before going back to college. And she suggested I go to New York. I had just turned seventeen. But you could go from Halifax to New York, there’s lots of ocean liners from Europe. It stopped in Halifax to let Canadian passengers off and there was quite a lot of empty state rooms, you could go to New York for about thirty dollars.
On a cruise? On a ship?

Yeah. And I went on that and my mother had worked there years ago as a secretary in a YMCA or something like that, and she told me how those people, it was laid out like a checkerboard, the numbered streets versus the avenues. And also I got arrangements that I could live at the YMCA on 23rd Street and Sixth Avenue for a dollar a night. And I also could eat in Horn, Harrod, those things, put money in the machine and get food out. They didn’t have a restaurant there. It was my first experience with a cafeteria. Because I went into the little place they had to eat food in the YMCA and sat down, nobody waited on me, and you had to find it. But during that time I went to shows. I went to the show “Sunny” in which the big hit song was “Who Stole My Heart Away,” and I saw the Earl Carrol Vanities and the George White Scandals. I went to a show called “The Great Temptations” and the orchestra leader, I thought I’d remember his name, it was something Castello or Don somebody. At any rate, one of the features was Jack Benny was a stand up comedian. This was 1926. But my first job must have been — no that’s right, the first year. But Jack Benny was funny of course. I’d never heard of him, but he had such a joke as “I went to this fine restaurant and I told the maitre d’ I says ‘what can I have for five dollars?’ And he says ‘let me shake hands with the head waiter.’” That was the joke. I did go to the opening game of the world series because I was a baseball fan. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

That was the series between the Yankees and the St. Louis Cardinals, and that was a famous ... I went to the opening game and sat in the bleachers for a dollar and ten cents, sat with a man who worked for the Diamond Match Company. I’ve never seen him since but he was very nice and he said “you coming back tomorrow?” And I said “yes I’d like to come again tomorrow.” “Well I’ll look for you here.” But he said “I live at the” some hotel. He said “come up to see me about eleven o’clock tomorrow, we’ll go together.” So I went up to this hotel to see him and got up to his room, and there was three other men with him, and they were playing cards. And I was playing cards, I was listening and waiting to go, and they got more interested in the card game and it went on and on. I don’t know that it was big stakes, just some kind of a game, social or not. And finally it got pretty late and I said “I think we’d better go.” And he said “well just a little longer.” And I said “I’m going to leave and take the street car up there to” — it must be Yankee Stadium. Well the first games used to be — well they all played in the Polo Grounds prior to that. So I went up there but that game was sold out so I didn’t get to go. Another thing happened in that year, I went over to Philadelphia because of the fight between Jack Dempsey and Gene Tunney. I was in Philadelphia on the 27th of September, 1926. I didn’t go to the fight but I listened to it on a radio in a drug store. It was a rainy night too. And of course Tunney beat Dempsey on a decision and that was questioned, they faught again and Tunney beat him again. But that was just part of my experiences in New York, going to these shows.
What was it about jazz music at the time that became — that you were so enamored of?

I don’t know. Words probably, the words are pretty good and they had a message to them. And Fred McClelland, my roommate, he’d say “I like this guy’s saxophone playing.” He explained to me the difference in sound on a record between a trumpet and a clarinet and a sax. And there was one funny sound that we used to get at that time, and he said “I wonder if that’s a bassoon?” Neither one of us knew. But one time he said “I met (some uncle) up in Twill the other day and he had an old instrument in there and I blew it and it wasn’t a bassoon, it was the bass thing.” But the bassoon is called the “ancient mariners” the nickname they have for musicians. But this funny sound that he had is what’s known as subtone clarinet. Have you ever heard of that term?
Sure.
Somebody that I’ve read about since perfected that style. It’s a funny, breathy sound but it’s a clarinet. And he didn’t know what that was.
Who were some of your big favorites in the 30’s?

I knew more favorites than individuals. I suppose that Coon Sanders, I loved to hear them play. McKinney’s Cotton Pickers was a jazz band. There’s a new one now in Detroit but this was the old one. I just knew the name, I never saw them. “It’s Tight Like That” was a © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -8-

jazz tune and “Rosetta” and numbers like that. And that was McKinney’s Cotton Pickers, not Coon Sanders. The Coon Sanders, they had a tune called “Deep Henderson” I’d never heard before, and I think there’s: Flamin’ mamie/The sure fire vamp/The hottest baby in town/She’s a heart scorcher/She loves torture/She loves to burn ‘em down. I remember those lyrics and that’s 70 years ago, but they made an impression evidently. I thought that people who write lyrics are bright, and that’s led my interest into them. Of the ones that I’ve met, the one that I am most fond of is Johnny Mercer. I met him by accident. Many of my things have been by accident, not by me looking for something. I became friendly with a bunch at Eddie Condon’s place. This was after the war and I knew most of them at the time when the band was Gene Schrader played the piano, Cutty Cutshaw played the trombone, Wild Bill Davis on the trumpet, and Walter Page on the bass and Eddie Condon on the guitar.
Walter Page, huh?

Walter Page. He had been with the Kansas City people and preceded Count Basie I believe. But he became a friend and he liked me. And I talked with these fellows and I would say “Walter, when you play with you and a piano and a drummer in a trio, and when you play a tune, you come to the end of eight bars, there’s a turnaround they call it to go back and some little fill in. And at the end of a tune you have a little something they called a turnaround.” And I said “you play, what you hear played that particular tune, that particular turnaround, but you don’t know what the piano player may do. He may take a sequence of chords or a chromatic ascension of chords or something.” I said “how do you know what he’s going to do?” He said “well doctor,” he said “you just know he’s going to do the right thing” whatever that meant. He’s dead of course, like most of those fellows.
Was the Condon bunch as wild as the books say?

Well yes, depends on what you mean by wild. He drank a lot you know, and I never said, he probably smoked marijuana, I don’t know. I heard him talk about “reefers” and “muggles” and things like that. I never had seen one. But as far as drugs, like narcotics, they never mentioned that to me or anything about it at all. I have had that experience later with more modern musicians that have talked about it, and solicited help that I couldn’t give.
So you saw them in Condon’s club? Was it Eddie Condon’s?

Yes. 47 West Third Street it was at first then they later moved to a club up on First Avenue and 40th Street or something like that, and then finally down next to where Jimmy Ryan’s was on 24th Street near the Sheraton Hotel. And by that time of course Ed Polcer became the manager. Now he was a player in the band years before that. I’m very fond of his playing. He comes to a lot of these parties. And he’s also graduated in © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-

business from Cornell or someplace like that. He’s a very bright person and a fine guy. They’ve all, those people have been so good to me that I just can’t believe it. But there’s nothing that I can give to them except friendship and they think they’re sympathetic that I like what they’re doing. They appreciate that.
Oh my. How has the music — the music we’re hearing today at festivals like this, do you think it’s stood the test of time? Do you think that the players of today are of the same caliber?
In what way? Quality or character or inspiration?
Actually, just in their musicianship I think.

I don’t think so. But maybe they know more than I do. They can take chords and it seems to me, if you understand a chord, you take the first, the third and the fifth and the seventh. C is the first, C, D, E is the second, F, G is the third, and B is the fourth and you flat the B it becomes a seventh chord. And above the B flat the next is D is the ninth and F is the eleventh, and A is the thirteenth, and back to C is the fifteenth. And I think some of these guys, they substitute chords. They play a chord in C but instead of playing the basic C they play the fourth, the sixth and the eleventh, and say what’s that. And they have such ear. I don’t know what they’re doing but that’s how they explain it.
That’s true.
And people like Thelonious Monk, I think he must be insane and yet there’s one tune I know he plays that I think is just a gorgeous thing called “‘Round Midnight.” You’ve heard of that?
Sure.

I think it’s very pretty. I’ve learned to play that by hearing him and another piano player wrote down lead line for it and it’s a gorgeous thing. And yet some other people have told me are the ones, “Ruby” is one I wouldn’t know it if I heard it. But this “‘Round Midnight” is a hit with me.
Beautiful. And tough, a tough tune too.
Yes.
It’s in a nasty key.
It’s in E flat.
E flat minor.

You can only play it — that’s another thing about — Zezz Confrey is one that I got interested in the early days. I heard him on records and of course the hit “Song Out Of Songs.” They called that novelty piano playing in those days. And his big hit was “Kitten on the Keys.” And everybody to this day knows about that. But he also wrote things like “Coaxing the Piano,” “You Tell “em,” I heard,” “Dizzy Fingers,” “Poor Buttermilk,” let’s see what. But so many. He wrote some little novelties, things that you would never © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -10-

believe came from him and called novelette, impromptu and romanza. And Dick Hyman has written and played those, and so did Dick Wells do it, who I got to know, who has now died, and Dick Hyman and a friend I met in Cleveland, a musician, had the music of those and he gave them to me and I learned to play those things. And you’d never believe that Sez Confrey could imagine those. But Confrey, his playing, we were talking about playing in different keys, if you played the piano, Confrey’s tunes could only be played in certain keys because they’re sliding from an F sharp to a C, down to a G and a B natural. And that’s how “Kitten on the Keys” goes. And you couldn’t play it in E flat, you only play it in this F. The same like “Dizzy Fingers,” it’s in the key of either D or A and it goes up. You could only play it in D, you couldn’t play it in another key without tremendous effort. It’s a funny thing about that. Those are trivial things that are not of much interest to anybody I don’t think, except maybe musical people would understand it, and you know what I’m saying.
Well but some of that music was definitely as hard to play as any classical music.

It is, yes. People that I admire that I used to listen to, my mother would have me listen to, was Rachmaninoff, hear him play his own things, and hear, a very interesting guy was DePackman, Vladimir DePackman. And he was a great — he loved to play Chopin music. And in those days records were made on wax and disks and so forth, and he’d become so enthralled in the music they tell me that he was playing some Chopin so meditatively, he’d say “oh that sounds so good,” and ruin the record and had to do it over again. And another, Alfred Corteau was a Swiss guy. I never saw him, but I had his records. And Olga Samaroff was a Polish girl who played a marvelous tune called “Sparkputz.” Other musicians tell me it’s a great favorite, a difficult tune. But I learned about those people and of course the other musicians I’ve learned that I’ve liked so much: Dick Hyman has been very good to me, and Dick Wellstood I got to know him, and also he had a big, he almost bled to death after a tonsillectomy one time and his wife was a nurse and was telling me about that so we talked about music in that case. And he’s one and there’s so many. Sajeen Shader was very nice to me, and one of the first I even spoke to when I went to Eddie Condon’s place. After each set played they’d go out and Ralph Sutton was the intermission pianist, and he’d be playing the piano, and the other guys would adjourn to the bar and they’d talk out there. In that same year I got the opportunity to get an orchestra and go and play in The Pines Hotel in Digby. That would be my last big shot at professional playing. And I had to write and tell Aunt Bess I wasn’t feeling well or something and tell the hospital that I was too ill, I couldn’t come. So I went to The Pines Hotel. And we had a saxophone player — two of them — my roommate that taught me so much, and another saxophone player from Halifax, and a drummer that was not a medical student but he played in so many bands at the college that even the professors thought he was a student, and a piano, and we had to have a violin. And I knew nobody in Halifax except some of the girls perhaps that could play violin really in tune. I knew Joe Venuti by hearing him but I said nobody can play like that. But I did get a man from a friend named Milton Karasek, who was from Boston. And we got in touch with him and he’d come down and work with us and play. He came over on a boat and you weren’t allowed to come in as a job so he had his violin and he had some other guy with a suitcase and he gave the violin © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

to another passenger to take it off and carry with the suitcase so they’d have no trouble with customs. But he was a great musician. What was your specialty in medicine — and is your specialty?

Well everything. I was a general practitioner, which included — and I went away to Cleveland, Ohio to get training in surgery. And one of the doctors in Cleveland was a successful surgeon and had trained at Charity Hospital in Cleveland. And he suggested that that would be a great place to go that it had a wonderful program, and also had a major league baseball team of course, and also at that time all kinds of jazz musicians © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

were there. And I couldn’t go wrong, so I said I’ll go there and take a year there at least, and I stayed the second year and I stayed the third year and then I decided I was going to stay there and practice there. So I would practice surgery, plus I had one month of obstetrical training besides, and so you did surgery fairly good, and obstetrics, and general medicine, until the war came along and then I went in the Army. I was still a Canadian but I went over in the American Army and was attached for a while to a place doing nothing, in Madison, Wisconsin, as a house doctor or something. Most of the patients were guys with flat feet or backaches or hangovers, things like that. They were fellows who were in the Air Force but had wanted to be pilots but were flushed out and wound up radio operators and radio mechanics, good jobs but they were frustrated. They were my patients. And then when they were preparing for the invasion in Normandy, they picked about four guys who were up there doing little or nothing and sent us down to join a group, the Fourth Auxiliary Surgical Group, which that became later, for the next war, the Mobile Auxiliary Surgical Hospital which is MASH. But we were the fourth Auxiliary Surgical Group. There were five of them and they were all made up of teams and the chief, the Colonel, said “what did you do in practice?” And I said “most everything, surgery and medicine.” He said “did you do any neurosurgery?” And I said “no.” He said “would you like to learn?” I said “yes, I would.” So he said “there’s a chief of a neurosurgical team that needs an assistant and maybe you could go with him.” So I went with him and he was bound to teach me and he taught me more in two years with him than I had learned in four years of medical school, how to do things. We did nothing but brain and spine injuries, twelve hours a day for two years. And you get to know how to do more than many people in civilian practice would ever see that many brain injuries we did. What I might have done after that was go back to medical school and learn about the rest of neurosurgery like tumors and stuff like that, but I decided I’d been away from my children for two years and my wife and I’ll do it next year and I’ll do it next year, and it faded away.
Was this overseas?

Yes. We went to England and lived in Evesham England for a while until June of 1943 we went to Normandy, to Utah Beach, a few days after it fell we went in the woods there, we went to a hospitals, field hospitals, evacuations hospitals, occasionally battalion aide stations, they were near the front, so they could get patients quickly. And the teams that we had, there were four neurosurgeon teams and there were about 30 general surgical teams, four thoracic surgical teams, four maxillo-facial surgical teams, and six orthopedic teams. We’d always be the same: the chief, the assistant, the anesthetist, two corpsmen and a nurse. And we always worked together, and different hospitals. You’d go and they’d put you in a truck with your equipment and go to some hospital, the front has © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

advanced so go up so you’re near them, and check in to the chief and he’d put you to work. We’d work 12 hour shifts. You’d do 12 noon to 12 midnight, and another team would take on the other hours, and it was a marvelous experience, and you just saw some awful things happen and I just think about those young kids, 19, 20, 21 year olds with terrible things happen to them, and the courage of those guys. It was nothing for us, we weren’t in any danger I don’t think. We had a red cross on our helmet and on our tents and everything like that and if there was any strafing of an area around there, I’m sure the Generals would avoid strafing a hospital area unless by accident. One time there was a lot of it going along at that time and my chief, the guy that was with me, said “do you think we ought to get under the table?” You’re just kidding I’m sure. But we decided no, the patient can’t join us so we’d better stay. Nothing happened though. We never had any trouble.

No I don’t think so. I was really excited. I was delighted. I thought I liked it. The people I was with were so great, the team. And those young men, the two guys, Eddie Jason was one, I haven’t seen him. He’s dead since then. But he came from Providence, Rhode Island. And he probably was a mechanic or salesman or something, and probably about 25 years old. Eddie Jason was his name. And he was just a marvelous little guy. The other fellow was Tony — I’ve forgotten it now, but I got in touch with him. Jason died not long after the war, some influenza or something. He finally settled in Nevada, in Carson City, the Capital of Nevada. I used to hear from him at Christmas, and he’d tell me how he was doing. As a matter of fact, I shouldn’t brag, but when I was installed as President of the AMA, I had written to him and he showed up to that thing, and what a joy to see him. I hadn’t seen him in about 50 years. And my son met him and he was just a marvelous, marvelous guy. And since then he died, and I’ve had notes from his children, how much he thought of me and how much they miss him. And some of the experiences like that, they’re just accidents, I’ve had so much good luck I can’t believe it. And the chance that I happened to see you. You happened to be talking to somebody, and I says there is somebody who likes music, and I tried to strike a conversation without butting in, and I found that you were. And I didn’t come looking to you for anything, it was just that I thought it was somebody who likes music.
Same here. You can tell when you’re in those kind of gatherings you know...

Yes, about that time. It’s when that new generation of new guys — I was interested in that. One of the things I learned in medicine, this has nothing to do with this so you may want to cut this out, but I was interested in medical politics and economics and I was on a committee from the Academy of Medicine from the labor union and from the hospitals and from the insurance industry in Cleveland. At that time they were planning about things after the war, and they established the fact that the commonest age for any woman in those age to have a baby was age 24. The war ended in 1945 and so there were a tremendous amount of young men coming back from war that would be getting married, they were positive in those later years, and so in 1946 these marriages would take place, and 24 years from 1946 was 1970. So they said 1970 — isn’t it 46, 56, yes, 24 years from ‘46 that it would be the biggest birth rate you’ve seen in years in the United States, and there’s going to be more hospitals necessary and more doctors necessary and so they said they had enormous programs. In fact Senator Burton from Cleveland, the Hill Burton Act, Senator Hill from Alabama, but the Hill Burton Act was enacted. Every town and community should have a hospital, they’ll need all these hospitals. And so there was a tremendous increase in hospital building about that time, from 1970 on. And in the late 70’s they wanted more medical schools they needed more doctors. And so at that time in 1974 or 5, there were 80 medical schools in the United States. And in the next 20 years they had 40 more medical schools. There’s now 126. And of course now they’ve got more than they need. They have so many that are in very elite specialties. A lot of guys go into that. Another thing they did was import people from other countries, deprived countries, they needed doctors there. So they allowed people to come here and stay and get training, but they want to go home to do good for their own country. And many of them did come, but when they got here they didn’t want to go home. The only way they could stay here was to marry an American girl, and a lot of them did.
